query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior at intermediate service temperatures emerges when thermally activated diffusion causes rapid nanoclustering of its principal elements (e.g., Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries, thereby reducing intergranular cohesion and predisposing the alloy to intergranular brittle fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20) with no preexisting grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Conduct a controlled tensile comparison at an intermediate temperature (around 700°C) under two different strain-rate regimes—one slow enough to allow thermally activated nanosegregation at grain boundaries and one high enough to suppress such diffusion.
generation.conditions: Testing at an intermediate service temperature (≈700°C) in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; all specimens start with the same homogeneous microstructure; one set is deformed at a low strain rate (providing sufficient time for nanocluster formation) and compared with a set deformed at a high strain rate (minimizing diffusion during deformation).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoclusters enriched in principal elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) that form along grain boundaries during prolonged exposure at temperature.
generation.mechanism: At intermediate temperatures and under slow deformation, enhanced atomic mobility drives the segregation (nanoclustering) of key elements to the grain boundaries. This accumulation reduces the grain boundary cohesive energy, promoting intergranular crack initiation and making the alloy behave in a brittle manner despite its initial single-phase, ductile microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under low strain-rate tensile tests at 700°C, specimens will exhibit increased intergranular cracking and lower toughness (brittle failure) relative to high strain-rate tests; concurrently, microstructural analyses (e.g., APT or TEM) will detect significant nanocluster enrichment at grain boundaries in the slow-tested specimens, while high strain-rate specimens will show minimal segregation and maintain transgranular ductile fracture.
generation.baseline: The initial homogeneous, single-phase HEA that shows favorable ductility (e.g., transgranular ductile fracture) under room-temperature or rapid-loading conditions.
generation.boundary: Service conditions defined by intermediate temperatures (≈700°C) and deformation rates that allow time-dependent diffusion; the test environment is controlled (inert atmosphere) to isolate the effect of nanosegregation without interference from oxidation or other degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of nanosegregation (i.e., the critical time or strain rate required for significant nanocluster formation) are not fully defined, and the relative contribution of these clusters to toughness degradation may depend on subtle microstructural details.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of homogeneous, single-phase HEA specimens. Split them into two groups for tensile testing at 700°C: one group at a low strain rate (allowing ample time for diffusion) and a second group at a high strain rate (minimizing diffusion). After testing, use high-resolution microscopy techniques (e.g., TEM and atom probe tomography) to quantify the presence and extent of nanoclusters along grain boundaries. Compare the fracture surfaces (intergranular vs. transgranular) and toughness metrics between the two groups.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves and fracture toughness values
Fracture surface imaging using SEM/TEM to identify intergranular vs. transgranular failure
Nanostructural and compositional analysis at grain boundaries using APT or high-resolution TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both low strain-rate and high strain-rate tests at 700°C yield similar ductile fracture behavior and negligible differences are observed in grain boundary chemistry (i.e., no significant nanocluster enrichment in the slow-tested specimens), then the hypothesis that thermally activated nanosegregation causes brittle behavior would be falsified.
